    ECG analysis

    Finds every R-peak in an ECG recording by matching each heartbeat against a QRS template, then turns the beats into heart rate and a rhythm category for triage. Pick a recording or upload your own.

    ECG strip

    Detected R-peak Atypical beat shape Reference annotation
    0.0 s

    Beat-to-beat interval (RR)

    Each dot is one beat. Spread means irregular rhythm.

    QRS template

    How the detector works

    1. Bandpass filter 5–15 Hz · removes baseline wander, muscle noise and mains hum, keeps the QRS
    2. First pass, Pan–Tompkins style · derivative, square, 150 ms moving average, adaptive threshold
    3. Build the template · median of the first-pass beats, 100 ms before to 150 ms after the R-peak
    4. Template matching · normalized cross-correlation; a beat must match above the threshold, reach 40% of typical R height and be 200 ms from the last beat
    5. Refine and summarize · snap to the sharpest point within ±50 ms, then heart rate, RR variation and atypical beats (match below 0.8)

    Send to triage

    Fills heart rate and the ECG category on the Queue tab. Add SpO₂ and blood pressure there to finish the reading.

    PPG analysis

    Finds every pulse in a PPG (pulse oximeter) recording: the systolic peak and the foot where each pulse wave starts. Turns them into pulse rate and a signal-quality score, then checks each pulse against the ECG heartbeat that caused it and measures the pulse arrival time used for PTT.

    Click a chart to move the strip there.

    How the detector works

    1. Bandpass filter 0.5–8 Hz · removes slow drift from breathing and movement and high-frequency noise, keeps the pulse wave
    2. Orientation check · an upright PPG rises faster than it falls; raw sensor IR is upside down and gets flipped
    3. Systolic peaks, Elgendi 2013 · square the positive part of the signal and compare a 111 ms and a 667 ms moving average; each block where the short one is higher holds one pulse peak
    4. Pulse foot · the tangent at the steepest upslope meets the level of the minimum before it; PTT is measured to this point
    5. Quality and rate · each pulse is compared with the average pulse (correlation 0.8 or more, amplitude 0.3–3× typical); pulse rate comes from the median interval between clean pulses
    6. Check against ECG · each R-peak is paired with the pulse foot that follows it at the typical delay; that delay is the pulse arrival time

    Send to triage

    Fills heart rate with the pulse rate on the Queue tab, and ticks poor signal on HR when fewer than 80% of pulses are clean.

    Scoring guide

    How each vital is scored, what the scores add up to, and where each value will come from once the sensors are built. Every vital gets a score from 0 (normal) to 3 (critical). Thresholds are adapted from NEWS2 and AHA guidance and are placeholders until reviewed by a clinical advisor.

    SpO₂ (blood oxygen saturation)

    The percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen. Low values mean the body isn't getting enough oxygen, which can come from blood loss, lung injury, or a failing heart. Future source: red and IR PPG sensor, using the ratio-of-ratios R = (AC_red / DC_red) / (AC_IR / DC_IR) and a calibration curve.

    ReadingScoreWhat it means
    96–100%0Normal oxygenation
    94–95%1Slightly low; watch for decline
    92–93%2Low; likely needs oxygen soon
    91% or below3Hypoxemia; critical on its own

    Blood pressure

    Scored mainly on systolic (top number). Low pressure suggests shock or major blood loss; very high pressure suggests a hypertensive crisis with risk of stroke or heart damage. Future source: automated cuff (oscillometric). Wrist or PPG-based BP is not yet reliable at clinical grade.

    ReadingScoreWhat it means
    Systolic 111–179 and diastolic under 1200Acceptable range for triage
    Systolic 101–1101Lower than ideal; watch for decline
    Systolic 91–1002Low; possible early shock
    Systolic 90 or below3Hypotension; possible shock
    Systolic 180+ or diastolic 120+3Hypertensive crisis

    Heart rate

    Beats per minute. Very fast rates can signal blood loss, pain, or an arrhythmia; very slow rates can mean a conduction problem or poor perfusion. Source: R-peak intervals from the ECG analysis tab (median RR), or the pulse rate from the PPG analysis tab, which also checks each pulse against the ECG.

    ReadingScoreWhat it means
    51–90 bpm0Normal resting range
    41–50 or 91–110 bpm1Mildly slow or fast
    111–130 bpm2Tachycardia
    40 or below, or 131+ bpm3Severe bradycardia or tachycardia

    ECG rhythm

    Suggested automatically by the ECG analysis tab from RR-interval variation and how many beats differ in shape from the QRS template, or entered by hand. The cut-offs below are placeholders for clinical review, and the result is a triage flag, not a diagnosis.

    CategoryScoreWhat it meansAutomatic rule
    Normal0Regular rhythm, consistent RR intervals, clear QRS complexesRR variation 15% or less and 5% or fewer atypical beats
    Moderate2Some irregularity, such as occasional extra beats, or a rhythm worth a closer lookRR variation 15–30% or 5–20% atypical beats
    Bad3Highly irregular or suspected dangerous arrhythmia (for example, possible AFib with a fast rate)RR variation above 30%, more than 20% atypical beats, or rate below 40 or above 150 bpm

    From scores to priority

    The four scores are added into a total (0–12). Reassessment times are proposals for the team to confirm.

    PriorityRuleWhat the responder does
    HIGHAny single vital scores 3, or total is 7+Immediate attention and transport first
    MEDIUMTotal is 5–6Urgent; reassess often (proposed every 15 min)
    LOWTotal is 0–4Can wait; reassess periodically (proposed every 30 min)

    Within the same priority, patients with a higher total score are ranked first.

    Trends and signal quality

    SituationWhat the system doesWhy
    Score rises by 2+ between readingsMarks Deteriorating and raises priority one levelA patient getting worse is more urgent than one stable at the same score
    Score drops by 2+ between readingsMarks Improving; priority follows the new scoreShows the patient is responding
    Poor signal on a vitalShows a Re-measure badge on that vitalMotion, poor perfusion, skin pigmentation, or bad contact can make readings wrong
    Value outside a possible rangeRejects the reading and asks to re-enterCatches sensor or typing errors before they affect ranking
    Scoring adapted from NEWS2 (SpO₂, systolic BP, heart rate) with an AHA hypertensive-crisis rule and an ECG rhythm category. Any single critical vital or a total of 7+ is high; 5–6 is medium. A patient whose score rises by 2 or more between readings moves up one level. Thresholds are placeholders pending clinical review. Sample ECGs from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (Moody & Mark, PhysioNet). Sample PPGs from NeuroKit2 (Makowski et al., 2021) and the PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2015 (Clifford et al.).
